Scale Distance

Source: R/kernel_dist.R
kernel_dist.Rd

Converts a kernel scale parameter (sigma) into a distance in map units: the distance within which a specified proportion of the kernel weight falls. Distances can be measured along a line through the point (one-dimensional) or as the radius of a circle around it (two-dimensional). Can be used with a fitted multiScaleR object to report optimized scale distances, or with manually supplied kernel parameters to explore kernel behavior.

Usage

kernel_dist(model, prob = 0.9, dimension = c("2d", "1d"), ...)

Arguments

model

A fitted multiScaleR object from multiScale_optim. When provided, scale distances and 95% confidence intervals are returned for all optimized covariates. When omitted, sigma, kernel, and (for expow) beta must be supplied via ....

prob

Numeric between 0 and 1 (exclusive). Cumulative proportion used to define the distance. Default: 0.9. The proportion refers to weight along a line for dimension = "1d" and weight on a plane for dimension = "2d".

dimension

Character. How the distance is measured. "2d" (default) returns the radius of the circle around the point that holds prob of the total weight the ideal kernel gives to locations on an unbounded plane. Because raster cells lie across a plane, the "2d" radius answers "within what distance does the ideal kernel assign 90% of its total weight?". For distance-weighted kernels it is larger than the "1d" distance; hard-radius covariates report the same radius for both. "1d" restores the original line-based distance, enclosing prob of the area under the kernel curve along a transect through the point. See Details.

...

Additional parameters used when model is not supplied:

sigma

Numeric (positive). The kernel scale parameter in the same units as the projection of pts and raster_stack passed to kernel_prep. For Gaussian kernels this is the standard deviation; for negative exponential kernels this is the decay length.

kernel

Character. The kernel function to use. One of "gaussian", "exp" (negative exponential), "fixed" (fixed-radius buffer), or "expow" (exponential power). Required when model is not provided.

beta

Numeric (positive). Shape parameter for the exponential power kernel. Required when kernel = "expow" and model is not provided. Ignored for all other kernels.

Value

When model is provided: a data frame with one row per optimized covariate and three columns, all in map units: Mean (distance at the estimated sigma), 2.5% (distance at the lower 95% limit of sigma), and 97.5% (distance at the upper 95% limit of sigma). Values are rounded to two decimal places. For hard-radius covariates (landscape metrics and unweighted surface metrics) the row reports the radius itself, whichever dimension is requested.

When kernel parameters are supplied directly via ...: a single numeric value giving the distance, in map units, at which the cumulative kernel weight under the requested dimensional definition reaches prob.

Details

Default change. Version 0.7.4 and later use dimension = "2d" for distances, summaries, and kernel plots. Earlier versions used "1d". Set dimension = "1d" explicitly to reproduce earlier reported distances. This changes reporting, not fitted sigma values, kernel weights, or likelihoods. Existing simulation extents, projection cutoffs, and optimization diagnostics retain their explicit 1D definitions.

One or two dimensions. A kernel assigns each raster cell a weight that declines with the cell's distance from the point. Two distances can summarize how far that weight reaches:

  • dimension = "1d" treats the kernel as a curve along a single line (a transect) through the point and returns the distance on either side that encloses prob of the area under that curve. For a Gaussian kernel the 90% distance is about 1.65 sigma.

  • dimension = "2d" accounts for locations lying on a plane, so the number of locations at distance d grows with the circumference 2 pi d. It returns the radius of the circle that holds prob of the ideal kernel weight. For a Gaussian kernel the 90% radius is about 2.15 sigma.

With sigma = 300 m, a Gaussian kernel gives a 90% distance of about 493 m in one dimension and 644 m in two. On an unbounded plane, locations within 493 m carry only about 74% of the total weight. When you describe the area associated with kernel weighting, or compare with values defined on the plane (for example, a radius holding 90% of the kernel weight), use "2d". Always state which definition you report.

Kernel formulas. In one dimension:

  • Gaussian: the inverse normal CDF, qnorm((1 + prob) / 2) * sigma.

  • Negative exponential: -sigma * log(1 - prob).

  • Fixed buffer: sigma * prob (the fraction of the buffer radius).

  • Exponential power: sigma * qgamma(prob, shape = 1 / beta)^(1 / beta); both sigma and beta (shape) must be specified.

In two dimensions:

  • Gaussian: sigma * sqrt(-2 * log(1 - prob)).

  • Negative exponential: sigma * qgamma(prob, shape = 2), about 3.89 sigma at 90%.

  • Fixed buffer: sigma * sqrt(prob), the radius of the circle holding prob of the buffer's area.

  • Exponential power: sigma * qgamma(prob, shape = 2 / beta)^(1 / beta).

Both definitions describe the ideal continuous kernel. They do not account for truncation at max_D, raster boundaries, missing cells, or cell geometry. The realized share of weight among extracted raster cells can therefore differ. If the two-dimensional radius approaches or exceeds max_D, consider increasing max_D in kernel_prep and refitting the model.

Confidence intervals for the fitted model case are derived from the Hessian-based standard errors (or profile-likelihood intervals when profile_sigma has been run and stored on the object). Each limit of sigma is converted to a distance with the same formula. For exponential-power kernels, beta is held at its fitted estimate during this conversion; the limits do not include uncertainty in beta or in site-specific retained weight.

summary() of a fitted model reports both distances; see summary.multiScaleR.

See also

summary.multiScaleR, plot.multiScaleR, plot_kernel

Examples

# \donttest{
## Using package data
data('pts')
data('count_data')
hab <- terra::rast(system.file('extdata',
                   'hab.tif', package = 'multiScaleR'))

kernel_inputs <- kernel_prep(pts = pts,
                             raster_stack = hab,
                             max_D = 250,
                             kernel = 'gaussian')
#> 
#> No sigma values provided...
#> Creating necessary elements to optimize sigma
#> 
#> Extracting values from raster layers...

mod <- glm(y ~ hab,
           family = poisson,
           data = count_data)

## Optimize scale
opt <- multiScale_optim(fitted_mod = mod,
                        kernel_inputs = kernel_inputs)
#> 
#> 
#> Optimization complete
#> 
#>  WARNING!!!
#>  The estimated scale of effect approaches or exceeds the current search extent.
#>  Consider increasing max_D in `kernel_prep` to >=250.56 to ensure accurate estimation of scale.
#> 
#> 

## Uses of `kernel_dist`
kernel_dist(model = opt)                     # radius of a circle (2D)
#>       Mean   2.5%  97.5%
#> hab 163.45 122.53 204.37
kernel_dist(model = opt, dimension = "1d")   # original distance along a line
#>       Mean  2.5%  97.5%
#> hab 125.28 93.92 156.65
kernel_dist(model = opt, prob = 0.95)
#>       Mean   2.5%  97.5%
#> hab 186.44 139.76 233.11
kernel_dist(sigma = 500, kernel = 'gaussian', prob = 0.95)
#> [1] 1223.87
kernel_dist(sigma = 100, prob = 0.975, kernel = "exp")
#> [1] 557.16
kernel_dist(sigma = 100, prob = 0.95, kernel = "expow", beta = 1.5)
#> [1] 235.51
kernel_dist(sigma = 100, kernel = "fixed")
#> [1] 94.87
# }

## The two definitions for a Gaussian kernel with sigma = 300
kernel_dist(sigma = 300, kernel = "gaussian")                     # about 644
#> [1] 643.79
kernel_dist(sigma = 300, kernel = "gaussian", dimension = "1d")   # about 493
#> [1] 493.46
